caseStudies.title: First Principles Thinking in Product Strategy
caseStudies.summary: Why breakthrough products often come from questioning the underlying need behind a process, rather than improving the existing way of doing it.
takeaways: Separating the underlying need from the traditional way of delivering it can unlock step-change innovation — e.g. separating 'matching supply and demand' from 'owning the assets involved'.
First-principles thinking isn't always a single flash of insight — some companies arrive at it gradually as supporting technology and infrastructure mature.

The same pattern — rebuilding a legacy system on new infrastructure — shows up across very different industries: communication moving off legacy telecom networks, payments becoming software infrastructure, manufacturing shifting to fundamentally different production methods.

caseStudies.title: Product Life Cycle Renewal
caseStudies.summary: Why some mature products keep growing after hitting saturation while others decline — and the different strategies behind renewal.
takeaways: Long-lived products often expand from a single product into a broader platform, but that only works when the expansion is a natural extension of the trust customers already have — not just an ecosystem play for its own sake.
Some products renew without expanding at all, by doubling down on price, distribution, and operational reliability — there's more than one path to longevity.
Failure to renew is frequently a strategic choice, not a capability gap — companies sometimes have the technology to adapt early but choose not to disrupt their own core business.

caseStudies.title: Product-Market Fit vs Market Readiness
caseStudies.summary: Why some well-built products struggle to gain traction while others take off — separating 'the product is good' from 'the market is ready for it'.
takeaways: A product can have genuine product-market fit within a narrow niche while still being blocked from wider growth by external factors like infrastructure, financing, or regulation — that's a market-readiness problem, not a product problem.

PMF benchmarks differ by category — habit-driven consumer products and trust-driven B2B products are validated differently, so outperforming your own category's baseline matters more than any single universal metric.
Being 'too early' is usually less about weak product-market fit and more about running out of time before the surrounding market catches up.

caseStudies.title: Mapping Critical User Journeys
caseStudies.summary: The gap between the user journey a product team designs and the journey users actually take — and how to decide which one to build for.
takeaways: Users frequently repurpose products for jobs the original team never intended — strong teams notice and sometimes lean into these emergent behaviors instead of only optimizing the 'intended' flow.
The journey most correlated with long-term retention isn't always the most common one today — it can be worth prioritizing a less-popular but higher-retention path over the high-traffic default.
Removing friction isn't automatically the right move — a longer, higher-intent onboarding can filter for the right users and improve long-term engagement, even at the cost of short-term conversion.
